extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and judges (readers of a 19th-century treatise on patent law)
extracted.subtask_short: assessing patent novelty and prior use
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating novelty and related defenses in patent law: when a patent is invalidated by prior knowledge or use, who counts as the 'first inventor', what constitutes 'use' or 'knowledge', and how reduction to practice, abandonment, or lost arts affect validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory novelty requirement: not known or used by others before discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Our statute requires that the subject-matter of a patent should not have been 'known or used by others before the discovery or invention thereof' by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase is interpreted to mean not known or used by others before the patentee's discovery (not merely before his application). It cannot mean not known or used by the inventor himself; use by the inventor to perfect the invention does not bar a patent. (See discussion of Act of 1836 and Pennock v. Dialogue.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of prior knowledge or use (U.S. vs England)
rubrics_metrics.description: In England, knowledge obtained at any time and by any mode before the application (or issuance) is sufficient to invalidate a patent; in the U.S., the relevant time is prior to the patentee's discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English law extends the disqualifying prior use down to issuance of letters-patent; U.S. law confines the inquiry to whether the invention was known or used by others before the patentee's discovery. This difference affects the treatment of prior uses long before an application or long-abandoned uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'others' — single prior user suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'others' denotes some person or persons other than the patentee; prior use by one person other than the patentee is sufficient to show the patentee was not the first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute's use of 'others' was intended to show the use must be by some other person(s) than the patentee, not necessarily by multiple persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes 'use' and 'knowledge' — product presence vs knowledge of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Raises the question whether the mere existence or possession of the product (machine, manufacture, composition) in another's hands before the patentee suffices to invalidate a patent, or whether the prior knowledge/use of the art or mode of constructing it is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is important when the product exists but the process or means of production has been lost or secret. For some subject-matter the art must have been known and in use; mere existence of a product may not always be enough to vitiate a subsequent patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior use when the art has been lost or abandoned
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention was once publicly used but later abandoned or the art of making it lost to the public, the effect on a subsequent patent is a distinct question from mere discontinued use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English authorities suggest prior public use, even if later discontinued, can invalidate a subsequent patent for machinery; but if the art has been wholly lost and not known to the public, a later discoverer of the process might still obtain a patent. Examples include encaustic tile manufacturing and glass staining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between machinery and processes (manufactures/arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a machine the invention consists in putting material parts together in a certain combination (which, once done, is always the same); in manufactures or products of an art the invention may lie in the process of production, which can vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a machine's structure is discoverable from inspection, prior existence of the machine often negates novelty; but for manufactures, the same product could be produced by different processes (secret or lost), so mere production of a similar article earlier does not necessarily defeat a later inventor's patent on his process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'first inventor' to allow patent to new discoverer of lost process
rubrics_metrics.description: On principle, where an art of making a thing has been lost, the phrase 'first inventor' ought to be construed to allow a patent to the new discoverer of a process of producing that thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports granting patents to those who are, so far as can be ascertained, the first inventors of their particular process when the earlier process is no longer known or usable by the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense available: patentee not original/first inventor or prior public description/use
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute declares 'the thing patented' is subject to defence that the patentee was not 'the original and first inventor or discoverer' or that 'it' had been described in some public work or had been in public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For arts, 'the thing patented' may be the process rather than the product; therefore, producing an earlier similar manufacture does not necessarily prove the prior knowledge or use of the patentee's process unless the earlier process itself is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee must be first inventor in point of time (U.S. stricter rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. statutes the patentee must have been the inventor first in point of time before all others; U.S. courts reject English distinctions that allow patents despite prior concealed inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. rule gives the first and true inventor the right to the patent even if his invention was known only to himself, provided it was perfected and put into actual use. Concealment by a prior inventor will not generally defeat the later patent under U.S. law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice / perfection required for prior invention
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute a prior invention that defeats a patent, the alleged prior inventor must have proceeded so far as to have been entitled to a patent had he made application — i.e., reduced the idea to practice and embodied it in some distinct form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere conception or speculative possibility is insufficient. In a race of diligence, the law recognizes priority of conception if the first inventor is using reasonable diligence to adapt and perfect the invention (see §15 qualification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere trials and experiments do not vitiate a subsequent patent; abandonment suggests only experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere trials and experiments, even if continued to the date of a patent, will not vitiate the grant if the patentee had no knowledge of them; abandonment of pursuit by the prior actor furnishes a presumption the proceedings were experimental only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior inventor abandoned the object for many years, courts view that as strong evidence that the prior acts were experimental and not a completed invention capable of defeating another's patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing experiments or lack of abandonment may suffice — fact question
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior actor continued experiments or there is no satisfactory evidence of abandonment, whether he achieved the same substantial result as the patent is a question of fact depending on the nature of the invention and results attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will examine the character and results of experiments to determine whether the alleged prior invention was complete and practically operative before the patentee's date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and burden — patent presumed valid until overthrown; proof strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff may rest on his patent as prima facie evidence of invention; the negative may be shown in defense. To prove novelty, witnesses 'in the way of hearing' are used to 'exhaust the affirmative instances' (prove they had never heard of it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have instructed that the defendant must overcome the presumption of validity; proof of prior invention should be convincing (jury instruction referenced requiring defendant to show prior invention beyond a reasonable doubt in one cited case). Calling persons who would have heard of the invention strengthens the patentee's evidence of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's own prior use before application does not defeat patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior use by the patentee himself, before his application, does not deprive him of his right to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language and judicial construction protect an inventor who has perfected and put his invention into actual use from being barred by his own prior use; the statute was meant to prevent others' prior use from defeating the first inventor, not to penalize the inventor for using his own invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence qualification (§15): priority where first inventor is adapting/perfecting
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute's §15 qualification provides that an inventor who invents first shall have the prior right if he is using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting the invention, even if a second inventor actually first perfected and reduced it to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a balance in races of diligence: priority in time of discovery/conception can trump who first reduced to practice, provided the earlier inventor exercised reasonable diligence to perfect the invention.
